prompt:

A. Human resource recruitment for the bakeries
B. Inbound logistics — receiving and storing wheat from farmers
C. Firm infrastructure — the company's accounting and finance function
D. Technology development — recipe and process research
model_answer: KEY: B — one mark. Marking points: (1) Primary activities are directly involved in creating and delivering the product — inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, and service — so B is the primary activity (1 mark, awarded only for B). (2) A, C and D are support activities (human resource management, firm infrastructure, technology development). No partial credit. Common slip: choosing D because research 'creates' the recipe — but in value-chain terms technology development supports operations rather than transforming inputs itself.

prompt:
PaperPrint (Pvt) Ltd, a Lahore-based commercial printing house, earns 70% of its revenue from printing university prospectuses, wedding cards and corporate brochures. (b) Identify two opportunities the same technology trends create for the company. (2 marks)

(b) Opportunities — 1 mark each for a credible opportunity linked to the same trends, e.g.: PaperPrint could offer its own on-demand app/portal; pivot to premium finishes and short-run packaging where digital print has an edge; sell design-plus-print bundles using the same AI tools. Award marks for analysis quality, not for matching these exact words.

prompt:
DairyFresh is a dairy-processing cooperative in Punjab selling pasteurised milk and yoghurt. Two large national brands are planning to enter its home districts, modern retail chains are squeezing supplier margins, imported milk powder remains cheap, and switching costs for consumers are low.

Required: Using Porter's Five Forces, analyse the competitive environment facing DairyFresh. (6 marks)
model_answer: Marking points (max 6 — about 1 mark per force, with the 6th for an overall judgement): (1) Threat of new entrants — HIGH: national brands entering with scale and marketing budgets; barriers such as cold-chain investment noted. (2) Bargaining power of buyers — HIGH: retail chains squeeze margins; end consumers face low switching costs. (3) Bargaining power of suppliers — MODERATE: cooperative structure gives some farmer loyalty, but milk is perishable and collection is localised. (4) Threat of substitutes — MODERATE/HIGH: cheap imported milk powder and UHT milk. (5) Competitive rivalry — HIGH: price-sensitive market, undifferentiated core product. (6) Overall conclusion — e.g. structurally unattractive unless DairyFresh differentiates (freshness, local brand, yoghurt innovation). Award for applying each force to the facts, not for textbook definitions alone.

prompt:

B. 14.0%

model_answer: KEY: C — one mark. Marking points: WACC = (0.60 × 18%) + (0.40 × 11%) = 10.8% + 4.4% = 15.2% (1 mark, awarded only for C). Distractors: A uses pre-tax-style misweighting; B is a simple average of the two costs; D overweights equity. No partial credit.

prompt:
The risk-free rate is 12%, the expected market return is 20%, and a share has a beta of 1.25.

Required: Using the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), what is the expected return on the share?

A. 20.0%
B. 22.0%
C. 24.0%
D. 27.0%
model_answer: KEY: B — one mark. Marking points: CAPM: Ke = Rf + beta × (Rm − Rf) = 12% + 1.25 × (20% − 12%) = 12% + 10% = 22% (1 mark, awarded only for B). Distractors: A ignores the risk premium; C doubles the premium incorrectly; D adds the full market return to the risk-free rate. No partial credit.

prompt:
Indus Engineering Ltd is financed by:
- Ordinary shares with a market value of Rs 120m
- 12% redeemable preference shares (redeemable in 4 years at par) with a market value of Rs 60m, currently trading at Rs 96 per Rs 100 nominal
- A bank term loan of Rs 40m at 3-month KIBOR + 2%; current KIBOR is 14%

Tax rate is 29%. The company's equity beta is 1.1, the risk-free rate is 13% and the expected market return is 21%.

Required:
(a) Compute the cost of each source of finance and the company's WACC using market-value weights. (4 marks)
(b) State one reason why this WACC may be unsuitable for appraising a proposed new software-services project. (2 marks)
model_answer: Marking points (max 6): (a) 1 mark each for: cost of equity via CAPM = 13% + 1.1 × (21% − 13%) = 21.8%; cost of preference shares ≈ IRR of Rs 96 now vs Rs 100 redemption in 4 years plus 12% coupon (accept approx 13.2–13.4%; preference dividends are not tax-deductible); after-tax cost of bank loan = (14% + 2%) × (1 − 0.29) = 11.36%; market-value weights 120 : (60 × 96/100 = 57.6) : 40 and the resulting WACC ≈ 16.0–16.3% depending on rounding. (b) 2 marks for a reasoned limitation, e.g. the WACC reflects the risk of the company's existing operations; a software-services project has different systematic risk (different beta) and possibly a different financing mix, so a project-specific discount rate is needed. Award for method, not exact decimals.
limitations: Self-marking rubric only — no official ICAP marking scheme exists for generated items. Figures are original; check arithmetic independently. Component-cost treatment (redeemable preference shares as debt-like) follows the standard textbook approach.

prompt:

(b) 2 marks: forward cost = 500,000 × 284.20 = Rs 142.10m, which is cheaper than the money-market hedge (Rs 145.10m) — recommend the forward, one reason being lower certain cost (accept the money-market hedge instead if justified, e.g. to avoid forward counterparty/credit-line constraints). prompt:

model_answer: Marking points (max 4): (a) 1 mark each for explaining: (i) futures — standardised exchange-traded contracts that lock in a borrowing rate; margin requirements and basis risk noted; (ii) options — the right but not the obligation to borrow at a set rate (a cap); premium cost, but the company keeps the benefit if rates fall; (iii) forward rate agreement — over-the-counter contract fixing the rate on a future loan; no premium, but the company is locked in and cannot benefit from falling rates. prompt:

B. IRR ignores the time value of money

model_answer: KEY: A — one mark. Marking points: IRR is defined as the discount rate that makes NPV equal zero (1 mark, awarded only for A). B contradicts the definition; C is false (IRR can be below the cost of capital — that is exactly when a project is rejected); D describes a limitation of IRR, not its definition. No partial credit.

prompt:
Chenab Packaging Ltd must choose between two mutually exclusive machines. Each costs Rs 8.0m.
- Machine X: expected annual cash inflow Rs 2.6m for 5 years
- Machine Y: expected annual cash inflow Rs 3.4m for 3 years

The company's cost of capital is 14%.

Required:

(b) State the payback period of each machine. (1 mark)
(c) Recommend which machine to buy, giving one reason and one caveat. (2 marks)
model_answer: Marking points (max 6): (a) 1.5 marks each: NPV(X) = (2.6 × 3.433) − 8.0 = 8.926 − 8.0 = Rs 0.93m; NPV(Y) = (3.4 × 2.322) − 8.0 = 7.895 − 8.0 = −Rs 0.10m (accept small rounding differences). (b) 0.5 marks each: payback X = 8.0/2.6 = 3.08 years; payback Y = 8.0/3.4 = 2.35 years. (c) 2 marks: recommend X — positive NPV versus negative NPV for Y (1 mark); caveat — e.g. payback favours Y and X's inflows are spread over a longer, less certain horizon, and unequal lives make direct NPV comparison imperfect (1 mark).
limitations: Self-marking rubric only — no official ICAP marking scheme exists for generated items. Figures are original; check arithmetic independently. Discount factors: 5-yr annuity at 14% = 3.433; 3-yr annuity at 14% = 2.322.

prompt:
A company's board has imposed a fixed annual limit on capital expenditure that is lower than the total cost of all positive-NPV projects available.

Required:
(a) Explain the difference between hard and soft capital rationing. (1 mark)
(b) Explain why ranking projects by NPV alone can lead to the wrong choice when capital is rationed. (2 marks)
model_answer: Marking points (max 3): (a) 1 mark: hard rationing is an externally imposed limit (e.g. lenders will not provide more funds); soft rationing is internally imposed (e.g. management sets a budget cap). prompt:
Gujranwala Logistics Ltd operates a delivery van that could be replaced now or kept for one more year.
- If kept: operating and maintenance costs will be Rs 420,000 next year, rising 15% per year thereafter; the van could be sold now for Rs 900,000.
- A new van costs Rs 3,200,000, has a 6-year life, and annual operating costs of Rs 260,000.

The discount rate is 12%.

Required:
(a) Using the asset replacement cycle concept, compute the equivalent annual cost of the new van. (3 marks)
(b) Advise whether to replace now or keep the old van for one more year, giving one reason. (2 marks)
model_answer: Marking points (max 5): (a) 1 mark each: PV of new van's costs = 3,200,000 + 260,000 × 4.111 (6-yr annuity at 12%) = 3,200,000 + 1,068,860 = Rs 4,268,860; equivalent annual cost = 4,268,860 / 4.111 = Rs 1,038,400 per year; marginal cost of keeping the old van one more year ≈ 420,000 (next year's operating cost) + opportunity cost of the forgone Rs 900,000 resale value (accept a simplified comparison: 420,000 + 900,000 × 12% = Rs 528,000 vs EAC Rs 1,038,400). (b) 2 marks: keep the old van for one more year — its one-year marginal cost (Rs 528,000) is well below the new van's equivalent annual cost (Rs 1,038,400); replace when the rising maintenance cost approaches the EAC. Award for method, not exact decimals.
limitations: Asset replacement cycle (KR10) is a named 2025 knowledge reference with no dedicated past-paper history, and the syllabus does not assign it to a specific LO — mapped to KR and C (suggested). The one-year marginal-cost comparison is a simplification of the full replacement-chain analysis. Figures are original; check arithmetic independently. Self-marking only.
